items.title: A simple estimate of cloud drop diameters from photographs of optical glories
items.abstract: The angular radius 𝛾 of the red ring of an optical glory, a set of concentric colored rings observed in clouds in the anti-solar direction, is used to estimate cloud drop characteristic diameter as 𝑑 = 𝜆/𝛾, where we take 𝜆 = 0.650 μm. A photograph of a glory taken with an iPhone 12 mini camera from a commercial airplane with 𝛾 ≈ 0.043 = 2.5° yields 𝑑 ≈ 0.650 μm/0.043 = 15 μm. Based on Mie scattering calculations, we show that despite occasional departures, this “diffraction” estimate is surprisingly robust and nearly independent of refractive index. We argue that photographs of optical glories taken from commercial aircraft constitute a potentially vast crowd-sourced database that could supplement, when coincident, more advanced ground-based, airborne, and spaceborne lidar and radar observations, with machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) applications.

items.title: A Study of the Effects of Language on Large Language Model Responses and Human Perception
items.abstract: People often feel an idea more strongly in their mother tongue, and they soften a hard message so that the listener is not hurt. This study asks whether chat-based large language models (LLMs) handle hard messages with the same care in English, Hindi and Marathi. Ten industry situations, such as a rejected build, a loan denial and the removal of an engineer from duty, were given to ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini in the three languages. The 90 collected messages were scored with a concept-matched word list that has five harshness categories and four softening categories. The scores were Harshness H, Softening S and Net tone N = H − S, with content coverage and length as extra checks. Differences between models were large (Kendall’s W of 0.30 for N and 0.56 for S). Differences between languages were small and not significant after correction. Gemini wrote short messages with almost no softening (S = 0.06), whereas ChatGPT and Claude used courtesy, regret and offers of help. Gemini also left out more key facts in Marathi (82% coverage) than in English (94%). Each cell holds one response, the word list was built after reading the data, and no human rater was used, so the results are exploratory.

items.title: A STUDY ON THE SOCIO-ECONOMIC PROBLEMS AND CHALLENGES OF AUTO DRIVERS WITH SPECIAL REFERENCE TO PALAYAMKOTTAI, TIRUNELVELI DISTRICT
items.abstract: Auto drivers are an important component of the local transport system, providing short-distance mobility and last-mile connectivity in towns and cities. Despite their contribution, their livelihood is affected by irregular earnings, rising operating costs, long working hours, road and traffic conditions, occupational health risks and limited social protection. This study examines the socio-economic profile, working conditions and major occupational challenges of auto drivers in Palayamkottai, Tirunelveli District. The study covers 150 auto drivers in Palayamkottai, Tirunelveli District. Data are presented for all 150 respondents and analysed using frequency distribution and percentage analysis. Percentage analysis and frequency distributions are used to summarise the available information. The results indicate that most respondents are aged 30–40, work for 8–10 hours daily, own their vehicles and report daily earnings in the ₹500–₹1,000 category. Poor road conditions, joint pain, fatigue and work-related pressure emerge as important concerns. The study recommends improvements in road infrastructure, access to welfare and health services, affordable finance and occupational health awareness.

items.title: A survey of natural language interaction and environmental perception in intelligent robotics
items.abstract: Natural language interaction and physical environment understanding are two core challenges for improving the autonomy of home service robots. This paper provides a systematic review of the evolution from traditional robotic methods to embodied intelligence enabled by large language models (LLMs), vision-language models (VLMs), and vision-language-action (VLA) models. For environmental understanding, we review the transition from geometric maps to semantic representations and behavioral navigation, emphasizing the roles of semantic SLAM, hierarchical scene representations, and VLMs. For natural language interaction, we analyze the limitations of rule-based approaches and the advances enabled by LLMs in task planning, reasoning, and code generation. Unlike previous surveys focusing separately on perception or language interaction, this review establishes a unified taxonomy and analyzes representative LLM/VLM/VLA-based robotic systems. We further discuss emerging trends toward multimodal reasoning, language-guided action generation, and adaptive embodied intelligence, while identifying key challenges in generalization, real-time deployment, safety, and interpretability. Finally, future directions toward reliable and adaptive embodied robotic systems are discussed.

items.title: A Technology Creates Its Own Pedagogy: Learning as Conversation in the Age of AI
items.abstract: Keynote: II International Meeting of UNESCO Chairs in Open, Digital and Distance Education, "Transforming Higher Education: People-Centred Digital Technologies and Artificial Intelligence." Madrid, 18-19 November, 2026.Every educational technology proposes a pedagogy. Jupyter notebooks, for example, by weaving narrative with code, invited a way of teaching computing as storytelling and live exploration; because they are open source, they also encouraged the sharing of learning resources and became ubiquitous. Generative AI proposes a pedagogy too, and its default is troubling: shaped like conversation, in everyday use it reverts to an antiquated model of instruction, the delivery of answers. Students who use AI as an answer machine develop an illusion of competence: the feeling of understanding without its substance. In this talk, I return to first principles. With Piaget and Papert, learners construct knowledge; with Gordon Pask, understanding is demonstrated by explaining it back in conversation; with Andrea diSessa, literacy is a social infrastructure, not only an individual skill. Read together, they suggest that the question for AI in education is not whether students converse with machines, but who does the explaining. Drawing on my own failed classroom experiment with an AI tutor, and on the innovation that followed—a scalable oral assessment I call the conversational exam, which restores the learner’s voice—I will argue for using AI as an amplifier of human conversation, and for investing in educators as the designers of those conversations.

items.title: Accuracy- versus efficiency-driven artificial intelligence use: Purpose matters, yet user dehumanization persists.
items.abstract: Building on prior studies that have documented the dehumanization of the users of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, that is, the tendency for observers to attribute less humanness to individuals who use AI than to those who do not, the present research examines whether and how different AI use purposes (i.e., accuracy- vs. efficiency-driven use) influence this effect. We conducted four preregistered studies (total N = 1,270) spanning diverse professional domains. We observed that accuracy-driven AI use negatively predicted the dehumanization of AI users, whereas efficiency-driven AI use positively predicted such dehumanization (Study 1). Furthermore, accuracy-driven AI users elicited less dehumanization than their efficiency-driven counterparts did, a pattern that proved robust across both intuitive assessments of dehumanization (Study 2) and deliberative ratings of humanness traits (Studies 3 and 4). However, both accuracy- and efficiency-driven AI users were significantly dehumanized compared with non-AI users (Study 4), demonstrating that while purpose matters, AI user dehumanization persists. These findings extend the literature on the social cost of AI and offer novel insights into how human–AI interaction shapes interpersonal dynamics .
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Advance Care Planning for Older Hospitalized Patients in China: Perspectives of Patients, Caregivers, and Healthcare Professionals
items.abstract: Background Older hospitalized patients often live with multiple chronic conditions and face an increased risk of mortality. However, advance care planning (ACP) remains underused in China. Understanding the barriers to and facilitators of ACP among older hospitalized patients may inform strategies to support its implementation. Methods Between May and December 2025, we conducted semi-structured interviews with patients aged over 80 years, caregivers, and healthcare professionals at a Tertiary hospital in a city in western China. Interviews explored participants’ understanding of ACP, discussions about ACP, factors influencing patients’ engagement in or avoidance of ACP, and perceived strategies and support needs for promoting ACP. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis. Results We conducted 35 interviews with 5 physicians, 10 nurses, 10 patients, and 10 caregivers. Two of the 10 patients (20%) had completed an advance directive(AD). Twelve of the 15 healthcare professionals (80%) reported receiving regular ACP training. Four themes that affect the implementation of ACP were identified (1)Awareness of ACP and sources of information; (2) Psychosocial and contextual factors shaping ACP engagement;(3)Patient values and communication in ACP decision-making; and (4) Strategies and support for ACP delivery.limited patient and caregiver awareness, emotional strain, family disagreement, and differing views on the timing of ACP discussions as important implementation challenges. Participants emphasized the need for professional guidance and communication tailored to patients and caregivers. Healthcare professionals also emphasized the importance of enhanced training, adequate staffing, standardized procedures, policy support, and support from artificial intelligence. Conclusions ACP engagement was limited among the patients interviewed.patients and healthcare professionals also differed in their views on the timing of ACP discussions. Professional guidance and communication between patients and their families, as well as training and support for medical staff may facilitate the implementation of ACP.

items.title: Advances in data-driven taxonomy of innate immune cells
items.abstract: Single-cell technologies, coupled with powerful machine learning, have multiplied the number of named innate immune cell states faster than their biological features have been established. Innate cell identity is generated by at least four partially independent axes (ontogeny, maturation, response to microbial or damage signals, and tissue adaptation) that project onto a shared transcriptional space. Consequently, snapshot expression data alone cannot uniquely attribute an observed partition to any one of these processes. Data-driven taxonomy has been particularly effective where one axis provides a stable interpretative anchor, as in ontogeny-defined conventional dendritic cells, and faces greater challenges where several axes interact, as in granulocytes, tissue-adapted macrophages, and ILCs. Here, we assess what recent atlas and foundation model studies have resolved, identify independent biological validation rather than computational resolution as the current bottleneck, and propose an explicit evidence hierarchy for deciding when computational clusters should be considered bona fide biological entities.

items.title: Advances in Intelligent Forage Production: Multi-Source Perception, Yield Estimation, and Precision Operations
items.abstract: Forage production currently faces multifaceted pressures, including resource constraints, climate fluctuations, and escalating labour costs. Accurately and promptly acquiring data on forage growth status and translating it into operational prescriptions is crucial for enhancing forage utilisation efficiency and production sustainability. This paper presents a comprehensive review of intelligent forage production, focusing on multi-source perception, biomass and yield estimation, precision operations, and system synergy. To ensure a rigorous synthesis, a structured literature search was conducted across Web of Science, Scopus, and CNKI, covering publications up to August 2026. Firstly, the roles of ground-based, near-surface, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and satellite platforms in monitoring plant height, canopy structure, spectral characteristics, moisture, and nutrients are compared; this is then followed by an analysis of data acquisition and calibration methods across varying spatial scales and temporal resolutions. Secondly, strategies for biomass and quality estimation—based on vegetation indices, red-edge and short-wave infrared (SWIR) spectroscopy, canopy height and three-dimensional (3D) structure, as well as machine learning—are synthesised. Particular emphasis is placed on the impacts of soil background, spectral saturation, mixed-sward heterogeneity, post-mowing regeneration, and cross-regional generalisation on model accuracy. Furthermore, precision operation technologies, such as variable-rate irrigation, fertilisation, optimal harvest window identification, cutting control, baling, and autonomous navigation, are summarised. The prerequisites for synergy among perception, estimation, decision-making, execution, and operational feedback are also analysed. A key synthesized finding is that structural-spectral feature fusion only yields actionable precision gains when temporal synchronization and spatial scale matching are strictly enforced, and continuous simplified local calibration remains indispensable for cross-regional model generalization. Finally, the integration of open-access multi-source data, the fusion of physical models with artificial intelligence (AI), rigorous external validation, and farmer-oriented low-cost deployment are proposed as key priorities for future research.

items.title: Advancing Cardiovascular Toxicity Assessment of Environmental Chemicals: AI-Powered Phenomic Profiling
items.abstract: Environmental chemical exposure has emerged as an important contributor to cardiovascular disease. Despite the exponential increase in the number of chemicals detected in environmental and human samples, cardiovascular toxicity data remain scarce for the vast majority of these compounds. The intricate architecture of the cardiovascular system yields complex and heterogeneous responses to chemical exposure, whereas conventional cardiovascular toxicity testing approaches are plagued by critical drawbacks, including limited phenotypic end points, poor mechanistic implication, inadequate efficacy and accuracy, and a lack of dynamic functional readouts. To address these gaps, we introduce the concept of the cardiovascular toxicity phenome (CTP) characterized by the totality of observable cardiovascular characteristics or traits encompassing cellular morphology, tissue architecture, and functional performance, induced by hazardous chemical exposures. To facilitate efficient quantification of the complex phenotypic indicators derived from the CTP, we propose an integration of artificial intelligence (AI)-aided testing platforms to analyze multiscale data sets generated from cell-, tissue-, and organ-level observations, thereby delineating the hierarchical organization of the vascular network and dynamic patterns within the cardiovascular system. This emerging paradigm remedies the shortcomings of traditional assays and establishes a framework for new approach methodologies (NAMs) in bolstering the cardiovascular toxicity assessment of environmental chemicals.

items.title: Advancing Oral Health Equity in Shenzhen: A Collaborative Expert-Informed Framework
items.abstract: Oral diseases remain a public health challenge worldwide and disproportionately affect populations with limited access to prevention and care. In Shenzhen, rapid urbanisation, internal migration, and social diversity may contribute to heterogeneity in oral disease risk, preventive behaviours, and service utilisation, highlighting the need for prevention-oriented policies. To address this need, a multidisciplinary forum was convened in Shenzhen on 20 November 2025, bringing together academics, health policymakers, epidemiologists, and oral health professionals. Before the forum, background materials on local epidemiological data and published evidence were circulated. During the forum, participants deliberated on these materials and reached broad agreement on strategic priorities, which were then synthesised into a four-pillar framework. The aim of this article is to present this expert-informed framework and to describe its rationale and policy implications for Shenzhen. The first pillar focuses on governance and infrastructure, including the establishment of an Oral Health Prevention Collaborative Network to improve coordination across schools, community services, public health, and clinical care. The second pillar emphasises workforce development and public mobilisation through training for primary care and community-based personnel, as well as population-level health promotion. The third pillar addresses technology and evidence-based interventions, such as teledentistry, artificial intelligence-assisted screening, caries prevention with fluoride varnish. The fourth pillar promotes integration into universal health coverage by expanding coverage for preventive and essential dental services and reducing out-of-pocket costs for vulnerable groups. Together, these pillars provide a preliminary expert-informed blueprint for improving oral health equity in Shenzhen. The framework aligns with global priorities in prevention, primary care integration, and financial protection, and may provide a basis for further discussion in other rapidly developing urban settings, subject to local adaptation and evaluation.

items.title: Agentic Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare: A Scoping Review of Clinical Value, Safety, and Human Oversight
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Healthcare AI systems described as agentic may improve selected tasks, but gains can reflect models, information access, human support or complete intervention packages. We mapped clinical utility, safety and workflow consequences while distinguishing functional agency from evidence isolating its contribution. Methods: We searched PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Scopus and Web of Science, supplemented by citation searches, through 11 September 2026. Eligible evidence comprised original empirical journal reports of healthcare systems described as agentic or demonstrating potentially agentic functions. Two authors independently screened records, and two independently extracted data, with adjudication. All four authors jointly assigned analytical classifications after a five-report pilot. A structured critical audit and descriptive Clinical Agency Evidence Chain informed synthesis. The review was not registered. Results: The corpus included 123 reports; 90 were classified as core or bounded functionally agentic. Within this subset, technical task performance was the endpoint category in 44/90 reports (48.9%), and clinical decision/process outcomes in 33/90 (36.7%). Three randomised reports in the broader corpus assessed patient health outcomes: one core, one boundary/non-agentic and one indeterminate. All evaluated bundled interventions. Evidence isolating agency and following its consequences within the same comparison was limited. Safety ascertainment, intended-user error correction and whole-pathway workload were incompletely reported. External or temporal validation occurred in 6/90 reports (6.7%), with partial validation in seven others. Predominantly retrospective, simulated or offline evidence limited clinical inference. Conclusions: Intervention-level benefit must be distinguished from the incremental contribution of agency. Technical gains and local or estimated time savings do not establish patient benefit or reduced total human work. Mechanistic comparisons and prospective clinical evaluations address complementary questions. Adoption decisions should consider benefits, harms, implementation conditions and uncertainty.

items.title: AI Agent for Personal Productivity Enhancement.
items.abstract: This research paper presents the design and development of an AI-based personal productivity assistant aimed at improving task management, time organisation, scheduling, and productivity tracking. The proposed system provides a unified platform where users can manage daily tasks, set priorities and deadlines, schedule activities, receive reminders, and monitor task completion. The current prototype is being developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to provide a simple, accessible, and user-friendly interface. The paper discusses the problem of managing multiple responsibilities, existing approaches to digital productivity assistance, the proposed system architecture, development methodology, implementation status, and future enhancements. It also explores the potential integration of intelligent task prioritisation, adaptive scheduling, and personalised recommendations. The project aims to provide a foundation for a smarter productivity management system that can help students and working professionals organise their daily activities more effectively. As the current prototype is partially developed, further implementation and testing are required to evaluate its effectiveness.

items.title: AI Applications in Manufacturing: Optimizing Production Processes and Enhancing Sustainability in the Food Industry
items.abstract: This paper explores the integration of Artificial Intelligence into the manufacturing sector, focusing on its applications in process optimization, product design, and sustainability, with a particular case study on cream cheese production within the Greek food and beverage industry. Four main types of AI technologies—a.) Data Analysis, b.) Machine and Deep Learning, c.) Optimization Algorithms, and d.) Generative Models—are discussed in the context of their roles in manufacturing. These are applied to five major areas within the manufacturing industry: 1.) Design and Engineering, 2.) Process Monitoring and Control, 3.) Manufacturing Operations, 4.) Production Chain, and 5.) Supply Chain. A detailed case study is presented, which demonstrates the application of AI in optimizing the production process of cream cheese, aiming to reduce resource consumption and improve production efficiency. The results indicate a notable improvement in sustainability metrics, particularly in energy and water usage, while maintaining consistent product quality. This work demonstrates the transformative potential of AI in enhancing both operational efficiency and environmental sustainability in manufacturing processes.

items.title: AI as corporate communicator: the role of AI source transparency, trust, and engagement in brand advocacy
items.abstract: Purpose This study investigates the role of artificial intelligence (AI) as a corporate communicator and examines how AI source transparency influences message credibility, employee trust, employee engagement and ultimately brand advocacy. Specifically, the study explores both cognition-based and affect-based dimensions of trust and evaluates the moderating role of AI literacy in shaping employees’ responses to AI-generated communication. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative research design was adopted using an online survey questionnaire. Data were collected from 317 employees across different organizations who had experience with AI-mediated communication in their workplace. Structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4.0 was applied to test the proposed relationships and evaluate the conceptual framework. Findings The findings indicate that AI source transparency positively affects message credibility. Message credibility significantly enhances both cognition-based and affect-based trust, which subsequently increase employee engagement. Employee engagement was also found to positively influence brand advocacy. However, AI literacy showed an unexpected negative moderating effect on the relationship between message credibility and cognition-based trust, suggesting that employees with greater AI knowledge become more critical and skeptical of AI-generated content, whereas its moderating effect on the relationship between message credibility and affect-based trust is not statistically significant. Practical implications Organizations should not use AI solely as an automation tool but also as a strategic communication instrument. Transparency regarding AI usage, combined with human oversight and quality assurance mechanisms, can strengthen credibility and trust. Companies should also invest in content governance and monitoring practices to ensure that AI-generated communication remains accurate, relevant, and aligned with organizational values. Originality/value This study contributes to the growing literature on AI-mediated corporate communication by developing and empirically testing an integrated model linking AI transparency, message credibility, trust, engagement and brand advocacy. It also provides novel insights into the complex role of AI literacy in influencing employee perceptions and trust toward AI-generated communication.

items.title: AI Legal Assistant for Saudi Commercial Law
items.abstract: Access to legal information in Saudi Arabia remains challenging despite the public availability of its laws, particularly in commercial disputes where relevant provisions are distributed across multiple legal frameworks and expressed in formal language that can be difficult for non-specialists to interpret. This paper presents an AI-powered legal advisory system for Saudi commercial cases that uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to provide legal guidance grounded directly in statutory text. Given a complaint written in natural Arabic, the system identifies the relevant Saudi laws, retrieves the applicable legal articles, and generates a structured legal opinion covering an analysis of the case, a direct answer to the user’s question, the supporting legal provisions, the user’s rights, and an assessment of the strength of the user’s legal position. Unlike general-purpose legal assistants, the system does not rely on unsupported legal knowledge or attempt to predict judicial outcomes; its substantive claims are grounded in retrieved legal provisions. The system was evaluated on 200 real commercial cases from the Saudi Ministry of Justice judicial portal, for which actual court rulings and judge-cited articles were available as references. Three independent large language models—Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeek, and GPT-4o—were tested as candidate generation models, achieving overall scores of 76.0%, 81.9%, and 87.0%, respectively. GPT-4o was selected as the primary generation model following this benchmark evaluation using different metrics such as retrieval coverage, article coverage, ruling accuracy, legal justification, and completeness. The results demonstrate the potential of retrieval-based legal systems to provide traceable and accessible legal guidance for Arabic-speaking users in the Saudi commercial law domain. The proposed solution has also been integrated into a live application, demonstrating its practical applicability and potential to provide accessible legal guidance to the general public.

items.title: AI Literacy and Learning Autonomy in Sustainable Higher Education: The Roles of Critical Evaluation, Responsible AI Use, and Cognitive Offloading Across Three Higher Education Systems
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping academic learning by enabling students to delegate cognitively demanding tasks, raising questions about the preservation of student agency and independent learning capacities within sustainable higher education. This study examines whether AI literacy is associated with learning autonomy primarily through critical AI evaluation, responsible AI use, and cognitive offloading rather than through a direct relationship alone. Survey data from 2111 university students in Serbia, the United Kingdom, and Germany were analyzed using structural equation modeling, serial mediation, and multi-group comparisons. AI literacy was positively associated with critical AI evaluation, which was positively related to responsible AI use. Responsible AI use was positively associated with learning autonomy and negatively associated with cognitive offloading, while cognitive offloading was negatively related to learning autonomy. Both serial indirect pathways were significant, whereas the direct association between AI literacy and learning autonomy was nonsignificant. No statistically significant differences in the examined relationships were detected across the three national samples. The findings extend research on sustainable AI-supported higher education by distinguishing technological competence from the evaluative and behavioral practices associated with student agency. They highlight cognitive delegation as an important dimension of the relationship between GenAI engagement and self-reported learning autonomy, offering insights into educational practices that seek to integrate technological assistance while supporting independent reasoning.

items.title: AI literacy in translation education: a qualitative evidence synthesis of critical translation judgement, pedagogy, assessment, and ethics
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is embedded in translation learning and professional workflows, yet translator education lacks an integrated evidence-based account of the knowledge, judgement, assessment, and professional responsibility needed for accountable AI-assisted translation. This study conducted a qualitative evidence synthesis of empirical research on AI literacy in translator education, using systematic searches of Scopus and Web of Science supplemented by citation tracking and manual searching. Professional-practice studies were coded separately to contextualise workplace responsibilities and conditions rather than to provide evidence of classroom effectiveness. The final corpus comprised 22 studies, including 18 core translator-education studies and four professional-practice studies. The synthesis identifies critical translation judgement as the organising capability of translation-specific AI literacy and integrates five dimensions across four curriculum-design domains: conceptual and technical foundations, situated pedagogical practice, assessment for accountable use, and ethical-professional positioning. The framework identifies equitable access and scaffolding, educator expertise, curriculum coordination, infrastructure, authentic project opportunities, and assessment capacity as cross-cutting implementation conditions. The findings support a shift from tool-centred AI literacy towards students’ ability to evaluate, verify, revise, reject, and justify AI-supported translation decisions while retaining responsibility for the final product. The evidence base is heterogeneous, limited to English-language publications, and geographically concentrated in East Asia, particularly China. This study synthesizes empirical research on AI literacy in translator education to establish an evidence-informed curriculum-design framework centered on critical translation judgment. By synthesizing 22 key studies across educational and professional contexts, the work provides educators and curriculum designers with a structured heuristic covering foundational knowledge, pedagogical practices, assessment, and professional ethics. Its significance lies in guiding a paradigm shift from tool-centered technical instruction toward fostering students' capacity to critically evaluate, verify, and justify AI-assisted translation outputs while maintaining accountability for the final text.

items.title: AI Readiness and the Future of Indian Higher Education: Connecting AI Acceptance, Self-Regulated Learning, and Digital Pedagogy
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming higher education by influencing teaching, learning, assessment, research, academic administration, and student support. In India, this transformation has gained particular significance following the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, which emphasises technology-enabled education, multidisciplinary learning, creativity, critical thinking, skill development, and preparation for an evolving knowledge economy. The emerging concept of Education 5.0 further emphasises human-centred, ethical, sustainable, and collaborative relationships between people and intelligent technologies. However, successful AI integration in Indian higher education depends not only on technological availability but also on AI readiness, technology acceptance, digital pedagogical competence, self-regulated learning, institutional support, and ethical awareness. This study examines the relationships among AI readiness, AI acceptance, AI-supported digital pedagogy, self-regulated learning, and learner engagement within the context of Indian higher education. A convergent mixed-methods design was employed. Quantitative data were collected through validated questionnaires from 250 higher-education teachers and students, while qualitative data were obtained through semi-structured interviews with 20 participants. Quantitative data were examined using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and multiple regression analysis, while qualitative data were analysed through thematic analysis. The findings indicate positive relationships among AI readiness, AI acceptance, digital pedagogy, self-regulated learning, and learner engagement. The qualitative findings highlight the potential of AI for personalised learning, feedback, academic support, and independent learning while also identifying concerns related to academic integrity, data privacy, misinformation, overdependence, unequal access, and institutional preparedness. The study proposes an India-sensitive framework in which AI readiness functions as a foundation for responsible AI acceptance and pedagogical transformation. The paper concludes that advancing Education 5.0 in Indian higher education requires coordinated investment in AI literacy, faculty development, digital infrastructure, ethical governance, inclusive access, curriculum transformation, and human-centred pedagogical innovation.

items.title: AI Readiness, Adoption, and Productivity: Firm-Level Evidence from Low- and Middle-Income Countries
items.abstract: Can firms in developing economies translate readiness for artificial intelligence (AI) into higher productivity and greater AI adoption? This paper develops Firm-Level AI Enablement Index (FAEI), a composite measure of Power Reliability, Digital Connectivity, Human Capital, and Institutional Environment. Using World Bank Enterprise Survey data for 44,251 firms across 76 low- and middle-income economies and a 2026 follow-up covering 3,579 firms in seven economies, the analysis examines the relationship between readiness, adoption, and productivity. The findings are as follows. First, the FAEI is strongly associated with labour productivity. A 0.1 increase in FAEI is associated with 11.5 percent higher sales per worker, conditional on country, sector, and survey-year fixed effects. Second, Human Capital shows the strongest positive association among the four pillars, followed by Power Reliability and Digital Connectivity. Third, FAEI is not consistently associated with AI adoption. However, firm-level digital practices, particularly website presence and electronic payments, are positively associated with AI adoption and several measures of AI engagement. Fourth, AI adoption is not significantly associated with productivity in the 2026 follow-up and readiness is no more strongly associated with productivity in industries with greater AI exposure. These findings highlight the heterogeneity between the capabilities associated with firm productivity and practices associated with AI adoption. For developing economies, strengthening Human Capital and foundational digital capabilities may be important priorities for improving firm performance and supporting AI adoption.

items.title: AI-assisted curriculum mapping for competency-based dental education: a comparative study
items.abstract: Curriculum mapping is essential for competency-based dental education but is often time-consuming and dependent on faculty interpretation. As dental schools undergo digital transformation, artificial intelligence (AI)-based tools may enhance curriculum quality assurance and alignment processes. Large language models (LLMs) may support curriculum alignment tasks; however, evidence in dental education remains limited. This study compared the accuracy, quality, efficiency, and faculty acceptance of ChatGPT-assisted versus manual curriculum mapping. A fixed-order, repeated-measures comparative study included 90 dental faculty members from Periodontology, Oral Medicine, and Oral Diagnosis. Participants completed manual mapping followed by ChatGPT-assisted mapping after a seven-day washout period, aligning course-level Intended Learning Outcomes with Program Learning Outcomes. Mapping accuracy against an independent, Delphi-derived reference standard was the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes included rubric-based mapping quality, task completion time, error patterns, and faculty perceptions assessed using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). The primary comparison used participant-level paired t-tests, with participant-clustered logistic generalized estimating equations used to assess incorrect mapping occurrence. Mapping accuracy was significantly higher with ChatGPT assistance than with manual mapping (78.8% ± 7.9% vs. 74.3% ± 8.2%; mean difference = 4.5% points, 95% CI 2.81–6.19; Cohen’s d_z = 0.56; p < 0.001). A secondary participant-clustered analysis supported this finding, showing lower odds of incorrect mapping (OR = 0.78, 95% CI 0.62–0.98; p = 0.035). ChatGPT-assisted mapping yielded higher rubric-based quality scores (25.67 ± 0.26 vs. 20.96 ± 0.36; p < 0.001) and shorter completion times (14.0 ± 1.5 vs. 27.8 ± 2.9 min; p < 0.001). The participant-clustered analysis found no statistically significant difference in the relative distribution of error types between methods ( p = 0.053). Faculty reported favorable technology acceptance, with all three TAM constructs rated significantly above the neutral midpoint (all p < 0.001). ChatGPT-assisted mapping was associated with significantly higher mapping accuracy, higher rubric-based quality scores, and shorter completion times than manual mapping. However, the fixed-order, non-randomized design precludes attributing these differences exclusively to AI assistance, as practice and familiarity effects may have contributed to the observed results. These findings support further evaluation of LLMs as faculty-supervised decision-support tools for curriculum alignment, particularly through randomized, counterbalanced, multicenter studies.

items.title: AI-Assisted Versus Immediate Unassisted Performance: A Quasi-Experiment in Tax Education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can improve students’ work, but an AI-assisted answer does not show whether they can reason alone. This quasi-experiment examined whether tax reasoning demonstrated with AI assistance was maintained when 41 Business Administration students reconstructed it independently. In a digital economy taxation case, the experimental group (n = 20) used the TaxDigital Tutor, an AI tutor developed for this study that guides reasoning without supplying answers, whereas the control group (n = 21) could use generative AI and other resources. All students immediately reconstructed their reasoning by hand without assistance, and both phases were scored with the same five-criterion rubric. Overall, scores were 14.3 points lower in the unassisted reconstruction (F(1, 39) = 18.39, p < 0.001). Scores declined by 17.9 points in the control group (p < 0.001) and by 10.6 points in the experimental group (p = 0.060); however, the exploratory between-group comparison was not significant (p = 0.282). Using case data as evidence was the lowest-scoring criterion in both phases. These findings suggest that scores obtained with AI do not necessarily reflect performance without it. The study also proposes the From Assisted to Autonomous (A2A) framework for progressively reducing AI assistance and assessing independent performance.

items.title: AI-Assisted Voice Analysis for Laryngeal Cancer: Primary Care Perspectives on Clinical Implementation
items.abstract: Background Voice-based artificial intelligence may offer a noninvasive approach to identifying patients at elevated risk for laryngeal cancer, but successful implementation depends on its acceptability and fit within primary care. This study examined primary care clinicians’ approaches to persistent dysphonia, perceptions of artificial intelligence–assisted voice-based risk stratification, and factors influencing clinical implementation. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional mixed-methods study using semi-structured interviews and an anonymous electronic survey that could be completed independently. Interviews explored dysphonia evaluation, referral practices, technology use, and perceived implementation considerations. Survey items assessed clinical reasoning using two dysphonia vignettes, technology readiness, application acceptability, and perceived barriers. Survey responses were summarized using descriptive statistics; no inferential statistical testing was performed. Interviews were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis, and qualitative and quantitative findings were subsequently integrated at the aggregate level. Results Fifteen clinicians participated in interviews, and 16 anonymous survey responses were received. In a clinical vignette of a patient with a smoking history who presented for persistent dysphonia, all respondents identified laryngeal or other head and neck malignancy in the differential diagnosis, compared with 12 of 15 (80.0%) for a similar clinical vignette without a smoking history. Thirteen of 16 survey respondents (81.3%) reported a positive or very positive initial impression of the proposed application, and 11 (68.8%) were comfortable or very comfortable integrating it into clinical practice. Interviews revealed that clinicians generally lacked a standardized pathway for escalating persistent dysphonia and viewed artificial intelligence primarily as decision support rather than a replacement for clinical judgment. Acceptance was conditional on demonstrated accuracy, minimal workflow disruption, appropriate clinician oversight, efficient referral pathways, and attention to equity, privacy, and accountability. Conclusions Primary care clinicians demonstrated interest in voice-based artificial intelligence for laryngeal cancer risk stratification, but willingness to adopt the technology depended on more than diagnostic performance. Successful implementation will require integration into existing workflows, preservation of clinical oversight, clear pathways from risk identification to definitive evaluation, and attention to patient trust and equitable access.

items.title: AI-Based Fake News Detection Using Natural Language Processing: A Review and Analysis
items.abstract: Misleading news often reaches readers before its claims can be checked, which has encouraged research into artificial intelligence (AI) and natural language processing (NLP) as tools for flagging content that needs closer examination. This paper reviews 31 publications from 2011 to 2024 and organises their approaches into four groups: traditional machine learning, deep learning, transformer-based models, and multi-source or real-time systems. It then tests one concern that recurs in the literature, namely that scores measured on one dataset do not carry over to another. Four standard classifiers (Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression, Linear SVM, and Random Forest, all on TF-IDF features) were evaluated on two public datasets: Fake or Real News (2016 political articles) and CoAID (2020 COVID-19 articles). Within Fake or Real News, five-fold macro-F1 ranges from 0.87 to 0.94. When a model trained on one dataset is tested on the other, macro-F1 falls to between 0.06 and 0.42. A model trained on an early CoAID snapshot also detects few fake articles in later snapshots, although the later test set holds only 15 fake articles, so that result is inconclusive. The highest-weighted terms of the linear models include source and formatting words, which suggests dataset-specific shortcuts. The paper also specifies CAMMS, a multilingual and multimodal framework with an explanation layer. CAMMS is described and given an evaluation plan, but it has not been implemented or evaluated here. The review finds no basis for naming one model family as best in every setting, and it points to cross-dataset testing, multilingual evaluation, transparent reporting, and human oversight as priorities.

items.title: AI-Based IoT Gas Leakage and Fire Detection
items.abstract: —Gas leakage, fire incidents, and abnormal envi- ronmental conditions create safety risks in homes, laborato- ries, workshops, and industrial settings. This paper presents RiskSense, an ESP32-based Internet of Things (IoT) prototype designed to monitor gas-sensitive readings, flame status, tempera- ture, and humidity. The prototype combines an MQ-2 gas sensor, a digital flame sensor, and a DHT11 sensor with local indicators, a buzzer, a motor driver, and the Blynk IoT platform. Sensor readings are processed using configurable thresholdbased logic for local alarms, while status values and alerts can be viewed remotely through a Wi-Fi-connected dashboard. An artificial intelligence (AI) layer based on a Random Forest classifier is implemented to classify the monitored conditions into NORMAL, WARNING, and CRITICAL risk categories. Isolation Forest for unusual sensor-pattern detection is proposed as future work. The paper describes the system architecture, hardware and software design, control logic, the Random Forest algorithm used, implementation methodology, validation plan, limitations, and future work. Since measured experimental results and numerical model-evaluation metrics have not been provided, no numerical performance claims are made. Index Terms—Internet of Things, ESP32, MQ-2, flame detec- tion, DHT11, gas leakage, fire detection, environmental monitor- ing, Blynk, Random Forest, machine learning.

items.title: AI-Based Predictive Civic Grievance Intelligence System
items.abstract: This research paper presents CivicWeave, an AI-based predictive civic grievance intelligence system designed to improve the identification, analysis, and prioritization of civic complaints. The proposed system analyzes civic complaints using their textual content, geographical locations, and submission timestamps to identify potentially related reports. It aims to help municipal authorities recognize recurring civic issues, understand complaint patterns, and identify incidents that may require greater attention. CivicWeave considers factors such as semantic similarity, geographical proximity, temporal information, complaint frequency, distinct citizen participation, citizen support, unresolved duration, and safety-related keywords to support incident analysis and priority assessment. It also incorporates a human-review mechanism through which municipal officers can review, approve, or reject suggested complaint relationships. The system is developed using React for the frontend, FastAPI for backend services, and MongoDB for data storage. It also supports optional Gemini-based text embeddings with a deterministic local fallback mechanism. The research focuses on improving civic grievance management through AI-assisted complaint analysis, incident identification, explainable prioritization, and human-centered decision-making. items.title: AI-Driven Environmental Monitoring for Aquaculture
items.abstract: This narrative review examines where artificial intelligence (AI) improves aquaculture environmental monitoring relative to conventional methods, how validation designs shape the interpretation of reported gains, and what evidence is needed for routine farm use. A thematic synthesis, supplemented by a targeted OpenAlex literature update, compares baselines, validation designs, and measured outcomes across water-quality monitoring, harmful algal bloom surveillance, contaminant sensing, and environmental management. In a flow-through farm, a neural time-series model improved imputation of influent dissolved oxygen (DO), while linear interpolation performed best for tank DO. In a separate six-pond evaluation within one farm, physics-guided transfer learning reduced the mean absolute error of nighttime DO forecasts by 35.5% relative to a standard long short-term memory model. In a 45-day pilot in one koi pond, integrated predictive control used 26.86% less energy than manual operation. These findings support task-specific use of AI for monitoring and decision support. Broader deployment of automated control requires independent farm validation and prospective assessment of water quality and resource use.

items.title: AI-Driven Tablet Manufacturing
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly optimising pharmaceutical formulation by enabling more precise, faster and cost-efficient drug formulation processes. Integration of AI technologies (such as machine learning and deep learning) with pharmaceutical formulation is commonly applied in drug formulation, including artificial neural networks (ANN) and logic systems. The integration of AI with formulation can predict drug behaviour, select excipients for optimisation, and design safer and more efficient dosage forms compared to traditional methods. AI-enabled instruments are currently employed across the pharmaceutical industry, in areas such as formulation optimisation, QC, and stability testing. Adoption of AI results in improved efficiency with data-driven decision-making and the ability to handle complex, multi-variable formulation problems; on the other hand, notable disadvantages such as high implementation costs, dependency on quality data, regulatory challenges, and the need for specialised technical expertise are observed. AI in pharmaceutical formulation has a wide scope in future, as it has the potential to revolutionise the production of medicine, accelerate novel drug delivery system design, and regulatory compliance processes. As AI continues to evolve, its role in pharmaceutical sciences is expected to expand significantly, bridging the gap between computational innovation and practical drug manufacturing, ultimately contributing to safer, more effective, and more accessible pharmaceutical products. This study comprises a detailed review of the application of artificial intelligence in pharmaceutical formulations, including the integration of existing technology with artificial intelligence.

items.title: AI-Enabled Technology in Digital Food Commerce: The Sequential Mediating Roles of Error Reduction and Psychological Empowerment in Frontline Employee Performance
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in digital food-commerce environments, where frontline employees interact with AI-enabled technologies to support transaction accuracy, service delivery, and operational decision-making. However, limited research explains how employees’ everyday work with AI-enabled systems translates into performance through operational and psychological mechanisms. Drawing on Conservation of Resources (COR) theory and Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) theory, this study examines the relationships between AI-enabled food-service technology, error reduction, psychological empowerment, and in-role performance. Survey data were collected from 410 full-time frontline employees, who evaluated the AI-enabled system they used in their own work, working in chain restaurants in Egypt using convenience sampling and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that AI-enabled food-service technology is positively associated with error reduction, psychological empowerment, and employee performance. Error reduction is positively associated with psychological empowerment and performance, while psychological empowerment is positively associated with performance. Furthermore, error reduction mediates the relationships between AI-enabled technology and both psychological empowerment and employee performance. Error reduction and psychological empowerment also sequentially mediate the relationship between AI-enabled technology and employee performance. These findings extend understanding of employee–AI work interaction in digitally mediated food-service environments by demonstrating how technology-supported accuracy and employees’ psychological resources are associated with effective task performance. The study offers theoretical and managerial implications for integrating AI into digital commerce operations while maintaining employee empowerment and effective human involvement in technology-supported service delivery.

items.title: AI‑Mediated Psychological Safety and Speaking Anxiety Reduction in University EFL Learners: A Qualitative Exploration
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a unique opportunity for language education. Speaking anxiety is one of the emotional barriers to learning a second language. As a result of advances in AI-mediated communication technology, second language learners can interact with AI systems through computer-generated conversational agents. However, there has been limited research on the effects of conversing with AI systems on students’ emotional responses, language learning behavior, and willingness to communicate (WTC) from a qualitative and learner-oriented perspective. In an effort to qualitatively explore how AI-mediated communication impacts learners’ sense of psychological safety and language learning behavior, this study recruited 80 undergraduate students who were enrolled in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) courses and had reported moderate to high levels of speaking anxiety. Participants completed four consecutive weeks of structured speaking tasks using the AI technology and completed reflective journals and semi-structured interviews. Reflexive thematic analysis was used to code the qualitative data to discern themes among participants’ responses and experiences. The study’s findings revealed that learners felt AI-mediated communication provided them with a psychologically safe, low-stakes space that led to less anxiety, more emotional comfort, and increased willingness to take linguistic risks. Learners also perceived themselves as taking more risks by using more complicated linguistic forms and feeling more comfortable communicating. The researchers from another study conducted by Jiaohui Tang et al. found that grit, self-efficacy for speaking English, enjoyment of speaking, and speaking anxiety were factors that had an effect on students’ WTC with AI. This can provide further insight into how psychological aspects of learners can impact language learning when AI is involved. From a pedagogical perspective, this suggests that technology like AI can act as a supplement to in-person instruction by providing a preparation space that encourages positive emotional and linguistic risk-taking.

items.title: AIGC Content Style, Posting Source, and Prosumption Intentions-The Mediating Roles of Perceived Ease of Use and Perceived Usefulness
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence enters social media marketing, content presentation and posting source have become key cues in users' evaluations of product recommendations. Drawing on the technology acceptance model, this study examines AI-generated content (AIGC) in text-and-image product recommendation posts on Xiaohongshu. It investigates the relationships of perceived anthropomorphic style, perceived informational style, and posting source with prosumption intentions, testing the specific and serial mediating roles of perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness. Three scenario-based studies were analyzed using regression and bootstrapping techniques to ensure robust statistical validation. The results indicate that both style perceptions were positively associated with prosumption intentions, and the official-source materials group reported significantly higher overall intentions than the individual-source group. Furthermore, models estimated separately for each style perception and posting source supported the specific indirect paths through perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness, as well as the serial path through ease of use followed by usefulness. For the product terms between each style perception and posting source, only the indirect path through perceived usefulness was supported. These findings explain users' acceptance of AI-generated product recommendation posts in terms of content comprehension and decision-related evaluations, offering practical guidance for content design and the assessment of marketing effectiveness in the digital era.

items.title: ALGORITHMIC GLOBAL VALUE CHAINS AND HIGHER EDUCATION TRANSFORMATION: RE-ENGINEERING INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS PEDAGOGY IN THE ERA OF AUTONOMOUS INTELLIGENCE
items.abstract: The rapid emergence of autonomous artificial intelligence agents, predictive supply chain orchestration, and real-time cross-border regulatory analytics is fundamentally transforming how multinational enterprises (MNEs) govern global value chains (GVCs) and enter foreign markets. Yet International Business (IB) higher education remains largely tethered to twentieth-century pedagogical paradigms—relying on static international trade models, retrospective written case studies, and essentialist cultural heuristics that fail to prepare graduates for algorithmically mediated global commerce. Moving beyond surface-level classroom adoption of generative chatbots, this study develops a comprehensive theoretical and operational framework for re-engineering International Business education through the lenses of Global Value Chain Governance Theory, Activity Theory, and Metacognitive Scaffolding. We argue that the defining competency for next-generation IB professionals is Algorithmic Value-Chain Orchestration—the ability to align predictive and generative AI systems with cross-jurisdictional institutional realities, geopolitical risks, and culturally grounded human judgment. To operationalize this capability, the paper introduces a Three-Horizon Curricular Transformation Architecture alongside a Synthetic Global Commerce Laboratory that immerses students in dynamic multi-tier supply chain disruptions, automated customs and rules-of-origin auditing, and cross-cultural digital platform governance. Drawing upon longitudinal pedagogical implementations across undergraduate and postgraduate IB cohorts, we demonstrate significant gains in students' systemic risk reasoning, critical verification of algorithmic outputs, and cross-border strategic adaptability. Finally, the study examines structural challenges—including cognitive atrophy, Western-centric training data biases, and cross-border data compliance—and establishes an institutional governance charter for sustainable business school transformation.

items.title: An agentic AI neutron scattering data scientist at the China Spallation Neutron Source
items.abstract: The interpretation of neutron scattering data remains a major bottleneck in materials discovery, as it demands an iterative cycle of data reduction, modeling, and refinement. That is too time-consuming for experts and too complex for novices. Here we introduce DrSai-Rongzai, an autonomous agent built on a large language model (LLM) that perfoms joint neutron powder diffraction (NPD) and pair-distribution-function (PDF) analysis without human intervention. Deployed at the China Spallation Neutron Source (CSNS), the agent orchestrates established refinement software through a hierarchical “Reasoning + Acting” framework. Its core innovation, Agentic Context Operation (ACO), maintains a coherent ‘working memory’ of file paths, intermediate results, and domain-specific rules across entire processing steps, even when the underlying large language model undergoes context compression. Across reference materials (Si, CsAgTe and Bi2MoO6), the agent refined structural parameters statistically indistinguishable from expert-derived solutions, while requiring markedly fewer iterative cycles. In an exhaustive 18-run factorial ablation study on two high-entropy alloys, we systematically evaluated the MemoWrite and CoreSkillWrite in ACO mechanisms with and without 50k-token context compression, quantifying the necessity of each component. Memo improved both mean composite performance and repeatability even without compression (+ 20.2% and + 11.3%, respectively). Under compression, Memo improved these metrics by + 10.7% and + 17.0%, and retaining CoreSkill provided a further + 12.5% and + 6.6% improvement, yielding a mean composite score of 0.9316 and repeatability stability of 0.9905 for full ACO. The agent is integrated with a permission-controlled CSNS data interface, enabling secure, on-demand analysis of user-proprietary data with automatic archiving. By combining rigorous benchmarking with practical, facility-ready deployment, DrSai-Rongzai demonstrates that autonomous AI agents can move beyond assisted recommendations to become reliable partners in complex structural science, potentially accelerating the rate of discovery at pulsed neutron sources worldwide.

items.abstract: This study presents an intelligent decision support system (IDSS) that integrates the extreme gradient boosting algorithm with the six-mechanism risk governance framework, which covers identification, assessment, warning, prevention, response, and accountability, for large-scale water diversion projects. Using real-time data from Internet of Things sensors, hazard logs, and management records, the system enables dynamic risk classification and interpretable early warning. Implemented in the Oujiang Water Diversion Project, the IDSS improves the timeliness of decision-making, strengthens proactive risk response, and supports the closed-loop tracking of high-risk events through human–AI collaboration. The paper also discusses practical limitations and provides guidance for deploying similar IDSSs in public infrastructure contexts.

items.title: An initial investigation into a low-complexity adaptive transparency framework for hearables using spectral analysis and loudness control
items.abstract: Transparency mode is an important feature of modern hearable devices, enabling real-time reproduction of environmental sounds while preserving perceptual comfort and situational awareness. Conventional transparency pipelines rely on static filtering and fixed loudness control, which perform poorly in highly non-stationary acoustic environments and often produce perceptual harshness, clipping, and unstable loudness behaviour. This paper presents an initial, proof-of-concept investigation into a low-complexity hybrid adaptive transparency architecture that integrates statistically driven loudness control, content-aware filtering, and lightweight acoustic feature analysis. Short-time energy and spectral centroid are jointly used to detect perceptually harsh high-frequency events and classify incoming acoustic frames. Based on this classification, harsh events are selectively attenuated through targeted band-stop filtering, while benign ambient sounds are preserved through gentle low-pass filtering. Loudness stability is addressed using an adaptive RMS-based limiter that dynamically updates its threshold via a combination of exponential moving average and percentile-based ambient estimators; this is a statistically driven loudness control strategy rather than a validated psychoacoustic loudness model. The proposed system is implemented in a real-time MATLAB framework that reflects the constraints of hearable-class digital signal processing. On a limited set of real-world environmental recordings, the proposed system shows lower peak-to-average ratio, improved transient handling, faster recovery, and smoother loudness trajectories compared to three static transparency baselines implemented for this study, alongside computational characteristics compatible with embedded hearable devices: an estimated per-hop cost of approximately 9000 multiply-accumulate operations. These findings are indicative rather than conclusive. This is a preliminary framework: perceptual evaluation was conducted informally by the two authors only, without an independent listener panel or a formal psychoacoustic loudness/sharpness model beyond the offline metrics reported, and the evaluation corpus was limited in size and diversity. Formal subjective validation and larger-scale, independently annotated evaluation are identified as essential next steps before broader claims can be supported.

items.title: An LLM-Based Multi-agent System for Digital Twin Integration in Industry 5.0
items.abstract: As we move from Industry 4.0 to Industry 5.0, fully automated systems start to give way to human-centric ones, in which human traits such as creativity and problem solving are leveraged and augmented through AI assistance. Human-AI collaboration is therefore fundamental. However, industrial processes are becoming increasingly complex. They are now hyper-connected ecosystems, integrating IIoT, AI, robotics or digital twins with new data streams and interdependencies. For a human, extracting and analyzing data from this complex ecosystem so that informed decisions can be taken becomes a non-trivial challenge. In this paper, we propose an agent-based architecture to interact with a Digital Twin, using FlexSim and a middleware layer as an interface. By leveraging the natural language understanding capabilities of LLMs, the system enables users to interact with the Digital Twin through intuitive, complex queries, democratizing access to data-driven insights and empowering human decision-making. A representative case study is used to provide an early validation of the middleware layer.

items.title: Analyzing Latent Manifold Paths Towards Geometric Transparency for Explainable 3D Point Cloud Generation
items.abstract: Explainability in diffusion-based 3D generative models remains limited, as their black-box nature obscures how complex geometric structures emerge from noise. Conventional post-hoc attribution methods, while useful for discriminative tasks, fail to capture the iterative, dynamic evolution intrinsic to the reverse diffusion process. We introduce Manifold Diffusion Explanation (MDE), a novel intrinsic framework that reinterprets denoising as traversable semantic paths along the Riemannian manifold of the latent space. By tracking and visualizing these geodesic trajectories—from isotropic Gaussian noise to coherent 3D objects (e.g., chairs, airplanes)—we demonstrate that object-specific generation is directly encoded in the manifold’s curvature and geodesic structure. This path-centric view yields transparent-by-design explanations rooted in the model’s internal dynamics, bypassing the need for external surrogates or post-hoc approximations. MDE thus bridges high-fidelity 3D generation with mechanistic interpretability, providing deeper insight into how diffusion models encode and unfold geometric priors. Our approach opens new avenues for trustworthy, human-aligned 3D generative AI in safety-critical domains.

items.title: Applications and Gaps of Generative AI in the Medical Device Lifecycle: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), including large language models, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and multi-agent systems, is used both as a tool around the medical device lifecycle and, less often, inside devices. These uses should not be conflated. This scoping review characterises current applications in design, regulatory management, maintenance, and risk assessment, and identifies where published evidence is thinnest. PubMed, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and arXiv were searched for 2022–2026 studies applying GenAI to hardware devices, SaMD, or medical wearables. Sixty-one studies were charted with the population–concept–context framework and mapped to the four pillars. Most included work is experimental. Reports cluster in regulatory document analysis and in risk or cybersecurity modelling. Live maintenance and generative hardware design remain sparse in this search. RAG and agent pipelines are commonly used to ground outputs, but published metrics are task-specific and do not demonstrate automated MDR or FDA compliance. GenAI can assist retrieval and drafting across the lifecycle, yet longitudinal real-world validation and human-in-the-loop controls are still scarce. In this corpus, operationally validated maintenance and in-device safety systems are the thin end of the map, not another document-mining prototype.

items.title: Aprendizaje Basado en Proyectos: camino hacia la motivación y el aprendizaje significativo
items.abstract: This article presents a methodological proposal grounded in Project-Based Learning (PBL), implemented in secondary education, with the aim of strengthening students’ intrinsic motivation, participation, and deep learning. The study was developed from a qualitative approach through participatory action research, which made it possible to analyze and transform the traditional pedagogical practices of seven teachers in a public educational institution located in a municipality in Colombia. The experience was structured in four phases: diagnosis, planning, implementation, and evaluation. The results show an increase in student motivation, greater cooperation among teachers, and a reduction in failure rates. Likewise, the findings indicate that PBL fosters the satisfaction of basic psychological needs—autonomy, competence, and relatedness—which are essential foundations of human motivation and enhance deep learning, knowledge transfer, and school persistence. Consequently, PBL emerges as a relevant pedagogical strategy for promoting holistic and humanizing education, capable of connecting knowledge with students’ real and meaningful contexts.

items.title: Are Cyber Teams Really Teams? A Comparative Review of Traditional and Cyber Team Performance Factors
items.abstract: Team performance has been extensively theorized in military, healthcare, sports, and organizational domains, yet the extent to which these theories transfer to cyber teams has not been systematically established. Through a systematic review of traditional team performance research and a structured comparison to the current cyber-team evidence, this study addresses that gap. We followed PRISMA 2020 guidance and extracted data from 267 primary studies published between 2015 and 2025 across organizational, project, sports, health care, military and technology-mediated team settings comprising 798 relationship records and 644 unique factor-pair associations spanning 60 standardized factors. The resulting factor inventory and relationship network were then compared against a published set of 42 cyber-team factors using a five-category correspondence rubric, which two coders applied independently (κ = 0.78 for cross-corpus mapping; κ = 0.84 for extraction). Findings demonstrate broad convergence at the factor level: communication, coordination, leadership, trust, shared mental models, and cohesion show strong conceptual correspondence across the traditional and cyber-team literatures, although their operational forms vary with technological mediation, temporal pressure, distributed work, and adversarial conditions. Several well-established traditional-team constructs remain underrepresented in cyber-team research. We integrate these results into a four-layer associative pathway model organizing structural inputs, mediating processes, emergent states, and multidimensional outcomes, and use it to identify where cyber-team theory should extend rather than replace traditional team science. Because the cyber comparison base is weighted toward software engineering, findings are most directly applicable to cyber-relevant technical teams but require further testing in security operations, incident response, and human–AI teaming contexts.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence & The United States Federal Government: A Policy Analysis of Governance, Private Sector Participation, and Public Value Across Administrations
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is no longer an experimental idea in Washington; it has entered everyday federal administration. Commercial vendors build the underlying models and data centers, while federal agencies act as buyers, users, and regulators. This paper examines how the federal government adopts AI, how private vendors shape that process, and how policy approaches shifted between the Biden and Trump administrations. While the Biden administration emphasized civil rights, risk mitigation, and structured safeguards (Executive Order 14110; OMB M-24-10), the Trump administration shifted the focus toward rapid deployment, regulatory relief, and commercial competitiveness (Executive Order 14179; OMB M-25-21). Drawing on public administration concepts like the principal-agent dilemma, vendor lock-in, and administrative burden, this study reviews real deployments across payment integrity, clinical documentation, drug review, and national security. The central lesson is that buying commercial software does not automatically create public value. To build an AI policy that supports both ordinary citizens and private enterprise, the federal government needs in-house technical capacity, open procurement standards to prevent vendor monopolies, practical testing based on real staff workflows, and clear administrative due process for the public.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Along the Supply Chain
items.abstract: Problem definition: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing production and operational models, yet whether and how AI technologies diffuse across economically linked firms, especially partners along supply chains, remains underexplored. Methodology/results: This paper documents the diffusion of AI technologies along supply chains where principal customers’ AI adoption significantly predicts dependent suppliers’ subsequent adoption. We establish the causal effect of this diffusion through rigorous and comprehensive empirical strategies that address endogeneity concerns, including placebo tests, selection tests, and an identification strategy based on the random H-1B visa lottery outcome. The diffusion mechanism is primarily driven by learning rather than catering, with suppliers acquiring specific AI applications from customers. The learning effect is stronger in relationships with higher relationship-specific investments and more frequent interactions. Suppliers experiencing AI diffusion achieve substantial economic benefits through quality improvement and cost reduction. Managerial implications: For corporate managers, our findings demonstrate that supply chain relationships serve as critical conduits for building AI capabilities, particularly for resource-constrained smaller suppliers, highlighting the strategic value of cultivating partnerships with technologically advanced firms. For policymakers, our results reveal supply chains as natural mechanisms for democratizing AI access, suggesting that policies supporting supply chain integration and knowledge sharing could accelerate the broader diffusion of AI benefits across the economy and society.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND HUMAN RIGHTS: INTERACTION, CHALLENGES, AND CONTRADICTIONS
items.abstract: The relevance of the study is due to the fact that the emerging information (digital) technologies, which are now an inevitable reality, have an impact on both society as a whole and the individual modern person, and in many cases have already become part of the latter's daily life. This process is manifested, among other things, in the widespread use of digital technologies, neural networks, intelligent systems, and so on. Artificial intelligence (AI) occupies a special place in this list. Today, there is hardly any area of society or human activity that is not affected by this technological advancement. This also applies to the legal sphere, one of the sections of which is the field of human and civil rights and freedoms. Taking into account the above, the goal of the research can be defined as a comprehensive analysis of all aspects related to: 1) the use of artificial intelligence in various spheres of the state and society; 2) the observance of human and civil rights in the context of the diverse and multifaceted use of AI as a factor influencing the observance of human and civil rights and freedoms both at the domestic and international levels. During our research, we concluded that it is necessary to create a clear regulatory framework that will ensure a balance between the use of AI, on the one hand, and the protection of public interests, as well as human and civil rights and freedoms, on the other. An example of such a framework, in particular, could be the legal regulation of artificial intelligence. By means of the said regulation, it is necessary to keep the process of using AI in various fields and spheres under constant control, and this process itself must be approached very carefully (as is the case with any achievement of scientific and technological progress): 1) to avoid the occurrence of negative consequences and side effects, 2) with the aim of clearly appropriate boundaries of the said use, 3) so that AI truly becomes a real assistant to humans, and not a substitute for human intelligence.
